tactics.claim: Mine your accumulated customer/client records to find what distinguishes your success stories from your failures, then codify those distinctions into a written list of red flags and green flags you can screen against.
tactics.mechanism: Six years of survey data contains the actual causal difference between customers who thrived and customers who struggled; distilling it into red flags and green flags converts accumulated experience into a repeatable filter that can be applied in a fifteen-minute phone call instead of discovered painfully over months.
tactics.evidence: Anecdote only: he describes spending a few hours a day for a week reviewing Strategic Profits surveys and compiling two lists. No figures, no sample size, no worked example of a red flag or a green flag — the promised list is deferred to later sections.

The client-screening application has no honest ecommerce form: a solo operator selling a $12 deodorant does not turn buyers away, and at ~54 orders/month the 'six years of surveys' input does not exist.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicates the top-vs-bottom decile contrast in marketing-performance-pattern-analysis and the best-customer work in marketing-retention-offers; the screening application does not translate to a 12-SKU consumable catalogue.

tactics.claim: The most valuable skill in business is the ability to create demand rather than find existing demand and fill it, because when consumer demand shrinks, sellers who only know how to sell into existing demand have nothing left to do.
tactics.mechanism: Most businesses follow 'find a need and fill it', which makes revenue a function of pre-existing market demand. When that demand contracts they have no lever. A seller who can manufacture demand for something nobody was asking for is not dependent on market conditions.
tactics.evidence: Assertion in a side-note, supported only by the claim that his own two products (BGS, GPS) had no demand until he marketed them. He explicitly defers the method: 'I'll be teaching you how I do it in future reports.'

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class (positioning), so age is not the issue — no mechanism is stated at all. He names the skill, claims it is the most valuable one, then defers. Nothing tells a solo operator what to write on a PDP, an Amazon bullet or a $30/day Meta ad. The actionable demand-generation work is already covered by marketing-awareness-level-messaging (unaware-buyer entry point, confronting line) and marketing-problem-solution-inventory.

tactics.rejectReason: Names a skill without supplying any mechanism; the executable portion is already owned by marketing-awareness-level-messaging and marketing-problem-solution-inventory.

tactics.claim: Stop buying tactics, tools and 'secret strategies' sold to entrepreneurs, because they supply new excuses ('I can't succeed without this traffic strategy / this video tactic / this software') rather than removing the ones you already have.
tactics.mechanism: Marketing aimed at struggling entrepreneurs is seductive rather than true. Each new tactic purchased becomes a new prerequisite the buyer can point at as the reason they have not succeeded yet, so consumption of tactics increases distraction and excuse-count instead of decreasing them.
tactics.evidence: Assertion only, delivered rhetorically ('I am shouting that'). No example of a specific purchase that produced an excuse, no data, no before/after.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class, age irrelevant. The underlying discipline is right for a solo operator at $2,700/mo, but the fleet already owns it with a procedure attached: marketing-performance-pattern-analysis Step 1 (name the binding constraint before critiquing anything, cap research) and marketing-paid-media-measurement (two-question triage, do-nothing on a working funnel, pre-commit the signals that license testing). This is an exhortation, not a rule you can apply to a decision.

tactics.rejectReason: Same conclusion as restraint rules already recorded in marketing-performance-pattern-analysis and marketing-paid-media-measurement, but with no mechanism or test attached.

tactics.claim: Your business results are determined by the quality of your thinking, so diagnose and fix your thinking process — accurate, clean, focused, correct thinking — before working on any business problem; the biggest leverage point in your business is you.
tactics.mechanism: Every result traces back to an initial thought, and difficult clients all shared a flawed thinking process that generated the surface problems they hired him to fix, so the surface problem can never be solved until the thinking is solved. Improving the single highest-leverage input produces a wave of downstream improvement, and can improve results with no change in behaviour at all.
tactics.evidence: Assertion plus quotations (Buddha, Henry Ford), the claim he can identify ideal clients in fifteen minutes on the phone, and that a 31-page report earned him $3.5M in funding. The four thinking categories and every named tool appear only as table-of-contents headings — none is explained.

rscFit.reasoning: This is the central thesis of the report and it is pure motivational framing as delivered. No mechanism a solo operator could execute: no exercise, no question, no artifact, no surface to change. It does not touch the Shopify PDP, the Amazon listing, the email flows, the $30/day Meta campaign, or the 18–22.5% repeat rate. The leverage-point half restates Step 1 of marketing-performance-pattern-analysis, and the claim that the leverage point is always the operator's thinking actively points away from the identified binding constraint, which is retention.

tactics.rejectReason: Untestable motivational thesis with no artifact, surface or decision rule; its one operational fragment (find the biggest leverage point first) duplicates marketing-performance-pattern-analysis Step 1.

tactics.claim: Make a diagnostic report required reading for anyone who wants to hire you, so preliminary work is completed during the wait and your paid time is spent only on the high-value work.
tactics.mechanism: A backlog means the seller's time is the scarce resource. Front-loading prerequisite work into a self-serve document that prospects consume while waiting means the engagement starts at a more advanced point, so expensive hours go to demand creation rather than remedial groundwork.
tactics.evidence: Assertion about his own practice ('this report will now be required reading for all companies and entrepreneurs who want to hire me'). No data on engagement length, conversion or outcome.

rscFit.reasoning: B2B consulting-practice operations — managing a waiting list for the founder's personal time. Real Skin Care sells 12 physical SKUs; there is no consulting engagement, no backlog of prospects buying the operator's hours, and no prerequisite work a buyer could complete before purchasing a $12 deodorant.

tactics.rejectReason: No honest translation at any size — it is service-business intake management, not ecommerce marketing.

tactics.claim: Information alone no longer confers advantage because it is abundant and free; your advantage comes from how you sift, evaluate and transform information better than competitors.
tactics.mechanism: The internet commoditised information supply, so the scarce input shifted from knowing to processing; companies that adapt fastest to the current environment survive.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class, so the 2010 date is not what sinks it. tactics.rejectReason: Macro observation with no prescribed procedure; the executable version already exists in marketing-performance-pattern-analysis.

tactics.claim: Never buy a 'business in a box' or done-for-you system; test any such offer by asking what happens when an entrepreneur in a low-cost country who will work harder for 1/100th of your target income buys the same thing.
tactics.mechanism: Anything that works purely mechanically and is sold openly gets bought by everyone, including operators with far lower cost bases, which drives price down until the advantage is worthless — and if it genuinely worked it would not be for sale at all.
tactics.evidence: Assertion plus a logical argument; no example of a system tested this way, no figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class (commoditisation logic). As stated here it is advice about which info products not to buy, which has no honest translation to a 12-SKU body-care catalogue, and it prescribes no test against RSC's own products or offers.

tactics.rejectReason: Advice about info-product purchasing with no ecommerce translation; the transferable commoditisation logic is already the differentiator audit in marketing-offer-construction.

tactics.claim: Because the brain is the body's largest energy consumer, it defaults to automatic processes, generalizations and habitual recall, so you must deliberately engage active focused thinking (observing, comparing, analyzing, evaluating, metacognition) rather than assuming you are already thinking.
tactics.mechanism: Evolutionary energy conservation makes not-thinking the default state; what feels like thinking is usually replaying a previously stored decision, so genuinely new conclusions require deliberate effortful attention.
tactics.evidence: Physiology figures (brain uses ~20% of oxygen and calories at rest vs heart 10%, lungs 10%, kidneys 7%), the claim chess champions lose 7–10 pounds of fluid in a two-hour match, plus driving and door-handle illustrations. No business outcome data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class (cognitive habit). The physiological story is interesting but the prescription is only 'think harder and more deliberately', with no procedure, trigger or artifact. The executable version of 'do not just replay a stored conclusion' already exists as Step 4 of marketing-performance-pattern-analysis — interrogate the execution before retiring an angle that 'failed before'.

tactics.rejectReason: Prescription reduces to 'think more deliberately' with no procedure; the marketing-shaped version is already Step 4 of marketing-performance-pattern-analysis.

tactics.claim: Diagnose your thinking against three roadblocks — flawed beliefs from faulty assumptions, fuzzy outcomes and sequences, and inaccurate maps of achievement — because roughly 80% of business results trace back to them.
tactics.mechanism: Faulty beliefs skew your point of view, fuzzy outcomes prevent you from separating essential from non-essential work, and inaccurate maps of achievement cause false paths and unrealistic expectations; fixing even one produces noticeable improvement.

What is here is a taxonomy of self-diagnosis with no test, threshold or artifact, and the one operationally useful idea (get clear on the outcome before deciding what work is essential) is already Step 1 of marketing-performance-pattern-analysis.

tactics.rejectReason: Taxonomy preview with the executable content withheld; its usable core duplicates the binding-constraint rule in marketing-performance-pattern-analysis.

tactics.claim: Before working on the business, run a written honesty audit of yourself: list the top five things you are pretending not to notice, answer a 26-question self-sabotage checklist, write down what those behaviours have already cost you, and project five years forward to what they will cost if unchanged.
tactics.mechanism: You cannot fix what you refuse to name — denial is presented as the single common factor across struggling entrepreneurs, so surfacing the behaviour in writing is the precondition for corrective action, and quantifying its past and future cost supplies the motivation to act. tactics.evidence: Assertion plus analogies (refusing to tell a doctor where it hurts, an alcoholic denying a drinking problem, a pilot waiting for divine intervention in a falling plane) and a claim that his analysis found denial in all the entrepreneurs who struggled. No data, no named cases, no outcomes.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class, so the 2010 date is not the issue. It produces no marketing artifact and no testable change to any surface Real Skin Care owns — it is a personal-psychology worksheet. Its actionable core (diagnose what is actually blocking you before critiquing assets) is already owned by Step 1 of marketing-performance-pattern-analysis in operating terms specific to this business, and adding a self-sabotage checklist alongside it would degrade triggering without adding a mechanism.

tactics.rejectReason: Personal-psychology worksheet with no marketing surface; the diagnose-before-acting core is already owned by marketing-performance-pattern-analysis Step 1.

tactics.claim: Prove the product works by naming individual customers (first name plus last initial) alongside their exact results, then turn the proof on the reader with a direct 'but what about you?'
tactics.mechanism: Named peers with concrete figures read as real people rather than marketing copy, and following the roll-call with a direct question at the reader creates a social-comparison discomfort that is supposed to convert into action.
tactics.evidence: Demonstrated rather than taught: 'Gloria L, Amanda K, Randy L did. They're already netting $43, $85, $32 per opt-in respectively', plus similar name-lists for two earlier reports. No results reported for the device itself.

tactics.rejectReason: Named-proof half duplicates marketing-conversion-copy-angles and marketing-review-mining; the guilt close is a retention risk at this AOV.

tactics.claim: When you are about to raise the price or withdraw an offer, announce it to existing customers and tell them explicitly that they are grandfathered in at their current rate.
tactics.mechanism: The same announcement does two jobs at once: for prospects it puts a real deadline on the current price, and for existing customers it converts a price rise — normally a churn event — into a loyalty reward. The locked rate becomes an asset the customer forfeits by cancelling, so commitment lengthens rather than shortens at exactly the moment a price change would otherwise trigger a review of the subscription.
tactics.evidence: Demonstrated, not taught, and stated twice in the same passage: 'we're going to be removing my reports from Founder's Club shortly (don't worry you'll still get them - you're grandfathered in)... we're going to be offering them at a much higher price... once again you're grandfathered in.' Assertion only, no retention or conversion figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class (retention and pricing psychology), so 2010 is irrelevant. Directly relevant because marketing-offer-construction already prescribes stepping prices upward in committed increments on Shopify, and this names what to do at the moment that step lands: email the subscribe-and-save base to say the new price applies to new subscribers only and their rate is locked. Free, one email, solo-executable, aimed at the binding retention constraint. Capped at 5 because it is close kin to the milestone-rate rule already in marketing-retention-offers — the additive part is narrow (the trigger is a price-change event rather than a tenure milestone, and the announcement itself is the retention mechanism) — because the recurring base here is small, and because the urgency half only works if the increase is genuinely honoured, the same failure marketing-scarcity-urgency-framing warns about.

tactics.claim: Anchor the perceived value of your offer by quoting a named authority's valuation of it ('Jay Abraham told me it should be a $10,000 a year subscription — and it would still be a bargain').
tactics.mechanism: A price stated by a credible outsider is harder to dismiss than a price you assert yourself, so the borrowed valuation resets the buyer's reference point far above what you are charging and makes the actual price read as a discount.

tactics.claim: Tell the reader the effort is front-loaded — that the hardest work is right at the start and that the workload falls while the payoff rises with every page.

tactics.evidence: Assertion embedded as a structural note about the report itself ('the effort this report asks of you is front-loaded... with each passing page your workload decreases as your payoff increases'). Not offered as a technique, no data.

tactics.rejectReason: Not advocated as a tactic, and its ecommerce translation is already owned by marketing-conversion-friction-audit and marketing-post-purchase-onboarding.

tactics.claim: Make an abstract point land by wrapping it in a vivid everyday analogy — refusing to tell a doctor where it hurts, an alcoholic denying a drinking problem, a pilot sitting motionless in a falling plane.
tactics.mechanism: Mapping an unfamiliar or uncomfortable idea onto a scene the reader already understands transfers the conclusion without requiring them to work through an argument.
tactics.evidence: Three analogies used in sequence in the text; assertion only, no comparison against a plain statement of the same point.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable copy-craft principle, but explaining a mechanism by analogy is already recorded in marketing-conversion-copy-angles as part of the three-pillar rule, with the body-care caveat attached (analogies in this category slide easily into implied physiological claims). A second weaker copy would degrade triggering, and the analogies demonstrated here are diagnostic-of-failure metaphors aimed at an entrepreneur, not at a buyer choosing a deodorant.

tactics.rejectReason: Already recorded in marketing-conversion-copy-angles with a body-care-specific caveat attached.

tactics.claim: Confront the reader directly and pre-warn that you may offend them, so they stop deflecting and recognise themselves in the copy.
tactics.mechanism: Naming the reader's avoidance out loud removes the exit route of dismissing the piece as being about someone else, forcing self-identification before the argument arrives.
tactics.evidence: Assertion, executed in the text ('I told you in the very beginning I might offend you', 'the entrepreneurs who'd benefit the most will be the quickest to give excuses why this report doesn't apply to them'). No data.

rscFit.reasoning: The usable core — call the reader out so they self-select — is already owned twice: 'Call your audience out by name in the copy' in marketing-conversion-copy-angles, and the sanctioned confronting line for an unregistered pain in marketing-awareness-level-messaging. The additive part, the pre-emptive offence warning, is a high-ticket guru register that overshoots for a $12 consumable at a $50.46 AOV where the spoken peer register is the recorded default.

tactics.rejectReason: Core is duplicated in two existing skills; the additive offence-warning register is wrong for this category and price point.

tactics.claim: Make the asset interactive rather than passive — build in blanks the reader has to fill in, and tell them the payoff depends on their engaging rather than just reading.
tactics.mechanism: Requiring the reader to produce their own answers makes them commit to conclusions they generated themselves, which raises implementation and therefore the results they attribute to you.
tactics.evidence: Assertion ('reading this report is not intended to be a passive experience... it calls on you to play an active role'), demonstrated by the fill-in exercises. No completion or outcome data.

rscFit.reasoning: The ecommerce translation is a worksheet or quiz lead magnet, already enumerated in marketing-offer-construction's three lead-magnet types (a scent/SKU match quiz is named explicitly) — and marketing-paid-campaign-structure explicitly argues to defer that quiz until a plain ad-to-page path has a baseline, because a solo operator cannot debug a multi-step sequence and a new ad account at once. Already recorded and already qualified.

tactics.rejectReason: Its ecommerce form (quiz/worksheet lead magnet) is already recorded in marketing-offer-construction and deliberately deferred by marketing-paid-campaign-structure.

tactics.claim: Rather than partially running five traffic strategies at once, get a quick overview of each, pick the single most promising one, commit to it and master it until it pays off — then reflect on whether the strategy or your execution was at fault before choosing the next.
tactics.mechanism: Spreading a single operator across many channels means being committed to 'getting something to work' rather than to making one thing work, so nothing is studied deeply, snags cause abandonment rather than diagnosis, and time and money are spent with no progress. Committing to one produces progress plus first-hand experience you can reflect on.
tactics.evidence: One hypothetical entrepreneur ('Joe') walked through blogging, SEO, Adwords, video and Facebook ads. Illustrative only, no data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class (focus discipline), so the date is not the problem — duplication is. marketing-acquisition-channel-selection already enumerates the channels a solo operator has and enforces running only the cheapest one or two until scale justifies more, and marketing-performance-pattern-analysis Step 4 already owns 'interrogate the execution before retiring the idea'. Adopting would restate two existing skills and blur the descriptions Claude Code matches against.

tactics.rejectReason: Both halves are already owned by marketing-acquisition-channel-selection and marketing-performance-pattern-analysis Step 4.

tactics.claim: Place explicit limits everywhere — cap yourself at three marketing strategies and focus on one, target one keyword instead of thirty, halve the hours you spend at the computer — because limitless operating is weak and self-imposed pressure is what forces you onto the few things that matter.
tactics.mechanism: With no ceiling on time or scope, an operator rationalises low-value work ('I'm going to be here all day anyway') and does many unimportant things; a hard limit creates pressure that forces the highest-value task to the front. Creativity seeks openness but productivity requires constraint — spreading finite effort across many targets means none receives enough to produce a result, so an artificial limit concentrates effort into something that can actually win.
tactics.evidence: One client anecdote: cutting his working hours in half turned a struggling business around. Plus a Dan Kennedy quote on self-imposed deadlines, the laser/light analogy, and the aphorism 'limits are the scaffolding that supports your success'. No figures.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class (operator discipline), age irrelevant. The marketing-scope half ('only three strategies, focus on one') is the same rule as marketing-acquisition-channel-selection, and the research-cap and restraint versions are already recorded in marketing-performance-pattern-analysis Step 1 and the do-nothing rules in marketing-paid-media-measurement. What is left — halve your working hours — is personal time management with no ecommerce artifact and no way to test it at ~54 orders/month.

tactics.rejectReason: Marketing-scope half duplicates marketing-acquisition-channel-selection and existing restraint rules; the remainder is personal time management with no marketing artifact.

tactics.claim: Stop blaming a lack of resources — time, staff, secret strategies, expensive software — and be resourceful instead, because it is never resources that stop an entrepreneur, only resourcefulness.
tactics.mechanism: Waiting for optimal resources is an excuse that postpones action indefinitely and wastes time on scavenger hunts; well-funded companies fail routinely, so resourcefulness rather than resource level determines outcomes.
tactics.evidence: Named third-party examples (Gates vs IBM, Walton vs K-Mart/Sears, Randolph vs Blockbuster) and the dot-com bubble as a counter-case. Anecdotal, no mechanism-level data.

rscFit.reasoning: Motivational framing with no stated mechanism a solo operator could execute or test. It names no artifact, no surface and no decision rule — 'be more like MacGyver' cannot be written into a PDP, an email flow or a $30/day Meta campaign. It also cuts against the fleet's stage discipline, which deliberately parks tactics needing people or volume rather than exhorting the operator to substitute grit for a media buyer.

tactics.rejectReason: Motivational framing with no executable mechanism, and it works against the fleet's stage-gating discipline.

tactics.claim: Cure 'destination disease' — stop fixating on the outcome, because when only the endpoint matters the achievement process is reduced to obstacles, which produces perfectionism, procrastination, paralysis and pessimism, and the daily work never gets done.
tactics.mechanism: Obsession with the destination kills the ability to enjoy the journey, which drains desire, passion and motivation, so the hard daily work required for business success stops happening.
tactics.evidence: Assertion, an Earl Nightingale quote, and a dig at Tim Ferriss's Four Hour Workweek plus an anecdote about Ferriss working sixteen hours over a weekend. No data.

rscFit.reasoning: Pure motivational framing with no mechanism a business can act on. The prime directive here is revenue, and this proposes no change to any surface, offer, flow or metric. Nothing about it is testable at any scale, let alone ~54 orders/month.

tactics.rejectReason: Motivational framing with no marketing surface, artifact or testable change.

tactics.claim: Reject the instant-success myth — no success is immediate and no failure is instantaneous, so stop hunting shortcuts, because the consistent search for shortcuts leads to large and disabling setbacks.
tactics.mechanism: Marketing, technology and entertainment all hide the repeated small steps behind results, so entrepreneurs expect an 'instant life', become preoccupied with shortcuts, and confuse speed with progress, adrenaline with purpose and urgency with importance.
tactics.evidence: Cultural observation (diet montages in films, internet-marketing 'overnight success' claims), a Gandhi quote, and the January gym-membership pattern. Assertion only.

rscFit.reasoning: Motivational framing with no mechanism — it prescribes no artifact and no decision rule. Where the fleet needs patience discipline it already has concrete, dated versions: the 10–14 day learning-phase freeze in marketing-paid-campaign-structure and the pre-committed degradation signals in marketing-paid-media-measurement, both testable in a way this is not.

tactics.rejectReason: No mechanism or artifact; the patience discipline it gestures at already exists in concrete form in the paid-media skills.

tactics.claim: Root out untested false beliefs: surface them by treating excuses, self-destructive behaviours and negative habits as clues, interrogate each with 'why?' repeatedly and 'what would I need to believe for this to make sense?', and write the answers down.
tactics.mechanism: Nobody acts without a reason or a payoff, so any behaviour that interferes with your goals has a hidden belief underneath it; working backwards from the behaviour to the belief that would make it rational exposes the belief so it can be disputed. A belief adopted without testing hardens into perceived objective reality and creates a filter that admits confirming information and blocks contradictory information, so the self-sabotaging behaviour it causes is continually reinforced.
tactics.evidence: Two invented worked examples (Jack, who reads self-help books without doing the exercises; Jennifer, who buys internet-marketing products compulsively) walked through the two questions. Illustrative only, no data, no case of a belief being tested and overturned.

rscFit.reasoning: The mechanism operates on the operator's private psychology, not on any marketing surface: it produces no copy, no offer, no image, no flow and no measurement. The 'five whys' structure is a general diagnostic that the marketing library already instantiates concretely — name the binding constraint, interrogate the production stack before retiring an angle — in a form that names actual artifacts (Klaviyo campaign history, PDP copy, static plates).

tactics.rejectReason: Self-coaching protocol with no marketing artifact; its diagnostic structure is already instantiated concretely in marketing-performance-pattern-analysis.

tactics.claim: Before accepting or acting on any claim from an outside source, run it through an explicit written skepticism checklist — separate the actual information from what you are inferring, ask whether the speaker has an ulterior motive or hidden agenda, whether there is sufficient evidence, whether this represents the common experience or an isolated occurrence, and whether any part of it is something you want to be true.
tactics.mechanism: Beliefs are acquired passively from whatever you read and watch, and humans draw conclusions automatically and unconsciously, so a single anecdote is silently upgraded into a general rule and a self-interested source is silently trusted. Motive, evidence sufficiency and representativeness are the three places a persuasive claim most often fails, and wishful thinking is what stops you checking — naming the thing you want to be true is what restores skepticism.
tactics.evidence: Assertion only — enumerated question lists (eight questions for misleading information, four for wishful thinking, four for jumping to conclusions) plus one illustrative example: wanting to believe others are 'crushing it' at adwords arbitrage. No data, no worked case of the checklist catching a bad claim, and the document itself is a sales piece for the author's own courses.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class (evidence evaluation), so the 2010 date is irrelevant. Free, purely editorial, and it lands on a real recurring failure here: almost every tactic in this library rests on an unquantified practitioner assertion — 'recovers up to 30% of abandoned carts', '50–60% of promotion sales land in the final hours', a 5% budget-scaling step, a $100/day ASC floor — each produced by a creator with an ulterior motive from an account nothing like a $2,700/mo solo operation. 'Is this the common experience or an isolated occurrence?' is exactly the question that stops an imported benchmark being treated as a forecast at ~54 orders/month, and it also governs reading the business's own small-sample numbers. Capped at 5 because it is a vetting habit rather than a revenue mechanism, it partially overlaps the existing discipline of running the arithmetic yourself rather than inheriting a rule of thumb, and the source offers no evidence the checklist works.

targetSkill.name: marketing-performance-pattern-analysis
targetSkill.description: Turning marketing data and outside claims into judgement: naming the binding constraint, tagging and contrasting assets, interrogating execution, and vetting imported benchmarks before acting on them.

tactics.claim: Stop sharing your good ideas with other people and write them on a list instead, so the pressure to implement builds until you act.
tactics.mechanism: Sharing an idea and receiving praise delivers the same psychological payoff as executing it, at a fraction of the effort, so each act of sharing drains the motivation to implement. Withholding leaves the payoff unclaimed, pressure accumulates, and the strongest ideas rise out of the growing list.
tactics.evidence: Personal anecdote — a transcribed instant-message conversation with a friend a year into his online career, plus his claim that he now keeps ideas to himself until he 'can't take it anymore'. No data.

rscFit.reasoning: Durable-principle class, but there is no honest translation to an ecommerce catalogue at any size: this is a personal motivation-management habit, not a mechanism that touches a listing, page, email flow or offer. The maintain-a-ranked-backlog half is already covered by the binding-constraint and capped-research rules in marketing-performance-pattern-analysis, which tell you what to work on next for reasons tied to revenue rather than accumulated psychological pressure.

tactics.rejectReason: Personal motivation habit with no marketing surface; the backlog half is already covered by marketing-performance-pattern-analysis.

tactics.claim: Generate as many ideas as you can, value-rank them, then choose and execute only the best one.
tactics.mechanism: Idea generation is a blessing only when followed by ranking and selection; without the ranking step the ideas spread you thin and cause direction-switching, which turns the same capability into a liability.

tactics.claim: Watch for the boiling-frog pattern of gradual decline and periodically self-audit by checking, for each area of your life and business, whether it is currently improving or declining — prospect knowledge, product quality, marketing effectiveness, overall business results, relationship with your list, reputation in the market — because there is no 'middle'.
tactics.mechanism: Gradual degradation is not perceptible at any single moment and effects lag causes, so level readings look flat and a business declines without any point at which the operator registers a threat. tactics.rejectReason: Gut-feel audit with no measurement basis; its marketing-relevant portion duplicates Steps 1 and 3 of marketing-performance-pattern-analysis.
